FIT.summary: You are a sophomore Aerospace Engineering major with foundational coursework in aerodynamics, vector calculus, and engineering mechanics. You have early technical communication and MATLAB skills, and you are targeting aerospace and mechanical analysis internships. The market data shows these roles demand strong engineering knowledge, mathematics, and design skills, typically at a bachelor's level or beyond. You have a solid start, but your profile is still developing for entry-level competition.

must_have_gaps.how_to_close: Complete a project where you design and assemble a small UAV or mechanism in SolidWorks, including dimensioned drawings and a simple motion study. Use a free online course like Coursera's 'SolidWorks 2024 Essential Training' or a university makerspace tutorial.
must_have_gaps.why_it_matters: In national occupational survey data for aerospace and mechanical engineering roles, Engineering and Technology knowledge scores a 94 out of 100, and Design knowledge scores a 78 or 88. Employers expect you to apply CAD in realistic engineering workflows, not just hold a certification.

must_have_gaps.how_to_close: Take a short course like MATLAB Onramp (free, 2 hours) and then build a project that simulates a simple control system (e.g., altitude hold for a drone) using MATLAB/Simulink. You can use the online documentation and examples.
must_have_gaps.why_it_matters: MATLAB appears as a hot technology in all three target roles. For aerospace and mechanical internships, national data shows Critical Thinking (78) and Mathematics (72) as must-have skills—MATLAB is how you'll demonstrate those in practice.

must_have_gaps.how_to_close: Complete a free introductory FEA module on ANSYS's learning hub or YouTube (e.g., 'FEA in 10 Minutes' series). Then, run a simple stress analysis on a SolidWorks part you design, documenting the mesh, loads, and results in a short report.
must_have_gaps.why_it_matters: For Mechanical Analysis Intern, analysis tools like FEA are tied to the must-have skill of 'Engineering mathematics' and the knowledge of 'Mechanical' (81 out of 100 in O*NET data). Employers want to see you understand FEA concepts even if you haven't used the software yet.

must_have_gaps.gap: FEA or analysis software (ANSYS, Abaqus) familiarity
must_have_gaps.how_to_close: Install the free student version of ANSYS or use the online ANSYS Learning Hub to run through a basic structural or thermal tutorial. Add a line to your resume: 'Completed introductory ANSYS tutorial for static structural analysis.'
must_have_gaps.why_it_matters: Hot technology lists for mechanical roles include many simulation tools. You don't need deep proficiency, but having any exposure shows initiative and fits the 'Computers and Electronics' knowledge (66 in O*NET data) expectation.

nice_to_have_gaps.how_to_close: Complete a free 2-hour course like 'Python for Everybody' (Coursera) or 'Learn Python 3' (Codecademy), then write a script that reads sensor data from a simulated UAV flight log and plots altitude vs. time.
nice_to_have_gaps.why_it_helps: Python appears in hot technology lists and Role Requirements for all three internships. It's a versatile tool for data analysis, automation, and scripting—differentiating you from peers who only know MATLAB.

nice_to_have_gaps.how_to_close: Run through the 'ANSYS Fluent Tutorial for Beginners' (available on YouTube or the ANSYS Learning Hub) that simulates airflow over an airfoil. Document the steps and results in a brief summary.
nice_to_have_gaps.why_it_helps: Even basic CFD exposure signals comfort with numerical simulation, which is valued in aerospace internships. National data shows 'Physics' knowledge at 76 for aerospace roles.

nice_to_have_gaps.how_to_close: Enroll in a free online module like 'Control Systems in MATLAB' (MATLAB Onramp) or watch a 3-part YouTube series on 'Control Systems Basics' by Brian Douglas. Build a simple Simulink model of a feedback control loop.
nice_to_have_gaps.why_it_helps: Flight Systems Intern specifically lists control systems as a must-have. Understanding PID control or state-space basics shows you can handle systems thinking—a differentiator that ties to 'Deductive Reasoning' (75 in O*NET data).

nice_to_have_gaps.how_to_close: Take a free short course like 'GD&T Basics' on YouTube or LinkedIn Learning. Then, apply GD&T symbols to a part you design in SolidWorks and include a note on your CAD drawing.
nice_to_have_gaps.why_it_helps: GD&T is a nice-to-have for all three roles. It shows you understand manufacturing communication beyond basic CAD, which fits the 'Production and Processing' knowledge (57 in O*NET data for aerospace, 84 for mechanical).

recommended_next_steps: 1. Complete the MATLAB Onramp course (free, 2 hours) this month, then build a simple Simulink model to control a simulated drone's altitude—this directly addresses the MATLAB/Simulink gap for Flight Systems Intern.

2. Start a project to design a small UAV wing or fuselage in SolidWorks, including a simple FEA stress analysis—this builds CAD proficiency and FEA familiarity simultaneously, targeting Aerospace and Mechanical Analysis roles.
3. Enroll in a free Python for Everybody module (Coursera) by next month—spend 1-2 hours to get comfortable with loops and data structures, then write a script that processes a flight log CSV.
4. Before the Fall 2026 semester, complete an introductory ANSYS Fluent or structural tutorial and document it as a short project—this adds a concrete simulation skill to your resume.

5. Once you finish the FAA Part 107 certification (expected Fall 2026), add it prominently on your resume—it's a unique credential that directly supports the Flight Systems Intern role and demonstrates regulatory awareness.
strengths: You've completed foundational aerospace engineering coursework (mechanics, aerothermodynamics, flight) and a math toolkit project that uses MATLAB basics, which shows you can apply theory to practical problems. Frame this on your resume as 'developed computational tools for vector calculus applications in aerospace contexts.'

Your SolidWorks CSWA certification and in-progress FAA Part 107 demonstrate proactive certification pursuit—two credentials that stand out for these roles and align with hot technology tools listed in national survey data.

Your analytical thinking and attention to detail (self-reported and evident in your course projects) map directly to must-have abilities like deductive reasoning and problem sensitivity, which are highly valued according to national occupational data.

data.role_evolution_summary: The aerospace engineering intern role is shifting from manual drafting and simulation setup to co-designing with AI tools. You're now expected to work alongside generative design software and AI-driven CFD platforms, making system-level thinking and AI fluency as important as classical fundamentals. For flight systems and mechanical analysis, routine tasks like telemetry processing, mesh generation, and first-pass FEA are being automated, freeing you to focus on higher-level interpretation and validation.

task_shifts.changing: Topology optimization in Siemens NX or ANSYS that used to require manual iterative CAD work is now handled by AI, proposing multiple structurally optimized geometries automatically.
task_shifts.meaning: Your engineering judgment to select and refine AI-generated designs—knowing why one topology works over another—becomes your key differentiator.

task_shifts.changing: AI surrogate models and agentic AI accelerate or replace many standard simulation runs, delivering predictions 10–100× faster than traditional solvers.
task_shifts.meaning: Your ability to interpret and validate AI outputs—spotting when a result is physically implausible—matters more than manually clicking through setups.
task_shifts.task: Setting up and running routine CFD simulations

task_shifts.changing: Processing test data, creating dashboards, and generating routine reports are now automated by AI analytics tools.
task_shifts.meaning: Your capacity to ask the right questions of the data and communicate insights clearly to engineers and managers becomes the value you add.

task_shifts.changing: AI-driven automation flags common issues before human review, so you spend less time checking standard specs and more on edge cases.
task_shifts.meaning: You can focus on creative problem-solving and non-standard challenges that require your human judgment.
